content: Dyspepsia, derived from the Greek words δυς(dys-, meaning difficult) and πέψη (pepse, meaning digestion), refers to chronic or recurrent pain or discomfort localized in the upper abdomen. This discomfort may manifest as mild pain, a sensation of fullness in the upper abdomen, or feeling full earlier than expected during meals. Additional symptoms may include bloating, belching, nausea, or heartburn. However, heartburn is excluded from the definition of dyspepsia in the ICD-10 classification, as it typically arises from different causes and requires distinct management approaches. Dyspepsia is a common condition, often linked to lifestyle factors such as smoking and dietary habits. However, it can also result from serious underlying conditions, including stomach cancer, peptic ulcer disease, or the use of certain medications. When dyspepsia occurs without identifiable risk factors for serious conditions, it is termed undifferentiated dyspepsia and can often be managed without extensive diagnostic investigations. If no specific cause is identified after thorough evaluation, the condition is classified as functional dyspepsia. The modern understanding of dyspepsia began with the description of gastric ulcer disease in 1799. The term dyspepsia in its current form was first introduced by Walter Alvarez in 1916. Dyspepsia is broadly categorized into two types: ulcer dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia, the latter also being referred to as functional dyspepsia. The symptoms of functional dyspepsia are primarily attributed to two key pathophysiological mechanisms: abnormal gastric motility and visceral hypersensitivity. These abnormalities may arise due to various factors, including early-life environmental influences, genetic predispositions, residual inflammation following gastrointestinal infections, or heightened stress responsiveness. Additional contributing factors include psychophysiological abnormalities, irregular gastric acid secretion, Helicobacter pylori infection, dietary habits, and lifestyle choices. Life-threatening causes of dyspepsia include coronary artery disease and ischemic bowel disease. More common causes encompass gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), gastritis, lactose intolerance, and peptic ulcer disease. Dyspepsia must be carefully distinguished from other conditions presenting with epigastric pain, such as acute pancreatitis, cholelithiasis, gastric outlet obstruction, myocardial infarction, and appendicitis. The incidence of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, a common cause of dyspepsia, varies significantly across populations. In developing countries, the annual incidence ranges from 3,000 to 10,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. The prevalence of H. pylori infection increases with age and is notably higher in certain ethnic groups and geographic regions. For example, in the United States, 20% of adolescents are infected, compared to 90% of children under five years old in developing countries. H. pylori-associated gastritis is more prevalent among African Americans, Hispanics, and the elderly compared to Whites. Globally, high rates of H. pylori infection are observed in regions such as Japan, Colombia, Costa Rica, and China, while rates are comparatively lower in the United States. Secondary prevention strategies for dyspepsia related to H. pylori infection include the use of antibiotics to prevent recurrence of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer. Post-treatment confirmation of H. pylori eradication is recommended using diagnostic tests. However, there is insufficient evidence to support routine screening for dyspepsia in the general population. Dyspepsia is typically a chronic condition with a low likelihood of spontaneous resolution. It is most commonly associated with H. pylori infection, and its prevalence increases with age. Persistent dyspepsia is linked to an elevated risk of developing duodenal and peptic ulcers. Complications of dyspepsia may include peptic ulcers, anemia due to gastritis, stomach cancer, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Despite its chronic nature, functional dyspepsia generally has an excellent prognosis, even in the presence of H. pylori infection. The clinical presentation of dyspepsia includes upper abdominal pain or burning, nausea, bloating, excessive burping, heartburn, a metallic taste, a sensation of fullness after eating, and discomfort in the xiphoid region. Some patients may experience chills, fever, or a feeling of something lodged in the esophagus. On physical examination, patients may appear pale, fatigued, or distressed. Vital signs are typically normal unless gastrointestinal bleeding is present, in which case tachycardia and pallor may be observed. Conjunctival pallor may indicate anemia, and halitosis may be noted in cases of chronic gastritis. Epigastric tenderness is a common finding, and stool tests may reveal occult blood in cases of gastric ulcers. There is no specific laboratory test for diagnosing dyspepsia. Laboratory investigations are primarily used to rule out bleeding, confirm the eradication of H. pylori after treatment, and evaluate refractory ulcers. Imaging studies are generally not required unless alarm features or risk factors for serious conditions are present. In patients over 55 years of age or those with concerning symptoms, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is recommended to exclude peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, and other potential causes. The treatment of functional and undifferentiated dyspepsia is similar. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are commonly used, although their efficacy in treating dyspepsia without heartburn is debated. Surgical intervention is not recommended for the management of dyspepsia. Primary prevention strategies for dyspepsia include avoiding long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), abstaining from alcohol, quitting smoking, reducing consumption of acidic or spicy foods, and managing stress. Adopting healthy eating habits, regular exercise, and maintaining a healthy body weight may also help prevent dyspepsia. Preventing H. pylori infection involves proper hygiene practices, such as handwashing, avoiding contaminated food and water, and minimizing close contact with infected individuals. Secondary prevention focuses on eradicating H. pylori infection to prevent recurrence of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer.
